blocks.x: I'll ask you what your name is first.
I'm Frank Netto, Jr.
Okay, we were talking, this is the second reel of Frank Netto, and you wanted to talk about a cello player?
Yeah, well, Maureen Lelke was the violin player, and shut it off.
Okay. You're saying the cello player's name?

It was Marcel Dorman, one of the finest in the country. He had that reputation. But he's known to Yo-Yo Ma, I don't think. And that's Al Fisher Hill. On bass. Yeah, on the bass. In other words, I took the tuba and took the picture with the tuba, so make room here. But that was a combination. This was the Hillcrest office. We used to play a program for them every Sunday. On WWL. On WWL, yeah. The staff orchestra.
What's a Hillcrest?
Hillcrest Dairies.
Dairies.
Yeah, they used to be the Hillcrest Farms and the Hillcrest Dairies. And we did the advertising. It was a half-hour program on a Sunday evening. For which I think the fee was something like about $6.
And this was when, approximately?

Well, it had to be before 34. Before 34. Yeah, yeah. Because 32, when the banks closed. When the banks closed. Really? About 32. About 32. When the banks closed. We stayed there, but we didn't stay too much longer. And Lelke was there. And Pinky was there. And they kept Lelke because they only had four or five people. And they let Pinky go.
May I ask you who some of these people are here? Yeah. Now, the tenor player on the left?
That's Nina Pecone. Mm-hmm.
And the fellow that looks kind of like he likes pork chops in the back?
Well, that's Tony Almerico. That's right.
And he acted like pork chops.

Yeah. And there's Dave Winstein. Yeah. And he's playing, what, alto? Yeah, he's playing alto. And Dave is a terrific musician. Never made a mistake, but he sounded like a punky goat. Uh-oh, a saw. I always kid him about it there. And there's Pinky Gerbrecht, you know, that name. Yeah. Elroy Mazur. Wyatt Schultz. Uh-oh. I met him in Jackson, Mississippi. He was a local official over there. He was a human in there. Yeah, he's still there. And there's Marino. And there's Marino. And there's Marino. And there's Marino. And Dave is a terrific musician.
Never made a mistake, but he sounded like a, uh-oh, a saw.

I always kid him about it there. And there's Pinky Gerbrecht. You heard that name. Yeah. He's still there. And there's Maureen Lelke. And there's Leo Addy on drugs. Oh, yeah, that's him. Uh, myself, Carl Martyr, Fisher, Steve Brew. He's the only musician in W, uh, Op Union that died during the war. He went over to the, went over the top there, D-Day. Uh-huh. And then when he took a rest, they threw a bum in the, in the place where he was sleeping. Killed Steve. Frank Pinero. Uh-huh. And I don't know who else she is. And, uh, Pinky Vodakovich. These singers, we used to swap them. They used to give them one. Well, she was a singer this morning. Yeah, she was a singer. And that violin player there?
No, that was a piano player.
Yeah, in other words.
But he had the bow. You see he doesn't have an instrument?
No, what's his name? Carl Lelke. All right, now. And there was, his piano, his violin player was Carl Marder and his wife Maureen Lelke
and Gurman.

That was the stringing song up there. And where was the picture taken? That's in WWL when it was in the Roosevelt radio station. And is it, did some of the guys double? It looks like it, looks like the Nina Pecone has a double. It looks like the Nina Pecone has a double. It looks like the Nina Pecone has a double.
It looks like the Nina Pecone has a double. It looks like the Nina Pecone has a trumpet next to him. I don't know why.
Would that be a vibraphone, that? He moved it on the side? No, it's a trumpet next to him.
I never heard of him playing trumpet. No, no, he never played trumpet. It must be Almerico's trumpet. Yeah, it must be Tony's.
An extra trumpet.
And I think I see a flute and a couple of Bames system clarinets.
Well, Dave played a little bit of flute. He brought it there to take the picture, I believe.
I think that Bames system.
Did you play any tuba with the owls ever? No. You didn't? No, no. Did you play string bass with the owls at the same time when Dan LeBlanc was around playing tuba?

No, no. I was on some bone now. And Dan, when the orchestra broke up, Dan went to school. He went to Loyola and became a teacher. Became a teacher? Yeah. He played too, he played too. What did he teach? Do you remember? He taught in St. Bernard Parish. He taught at school and the system there. Music? Yeah, he taught music. And I could never stand Lou Wap, why he didn't give him a job, with all of these funny yokels they had, you know, around there that he put on. And of course, Lou Wap, I don't want to say that. He's not one of my favorites. Did you ever play with him? Many of them. Not many, not many. I played for Stan Bow, you know, when Dick was there to take a night off, I played with him. He shoveled, you know, he shoveled it up there at what Truman calls fertilizer. You know, he'd throw it up there and throw it at you. And I told him, I said, I've made all of that before.
You played with Tony Amarico in that band. You played with him some other times too, didn't you?
Oh yeah, I played with Tony quite a while. On a boat at the Capitol during the war. Tony had a fine band on that boat.
And you played trombone with him or bass? No, no, I was on bass. You were on bass.
Trombone. Somebody stole the trombone. Somebody probably heard me play it and just stole it.
When did you stop playing trombone?
At the end of the owls? At the end of the owls, yeah. And you haven't played it since? No, I never did.
You played bass with the owls, though?
I played bass fiddle with the smaller owls. I see. But, no, I didn't play. No, Dan was, where's his other picture over there? I don't know where. Must be in here.

Well look for it and I'll talk about this picture. Yeah, well, here. I noticed Elrey Mace is playing the Albert System clarinet and he and Dave apparently double on baritone. They're playing alto. There it is, yeah. Okay. And here you are with the bass. Yeah, I had bass fiddle, yeah. In the small owls. Yeah. Good question. Well, what happened to Errol Crum?

Well, went into the electrical business with the football player, you remember, Irish Levy? No, I never heard such a name. Yeah, that was back in the, well, he was the famous guard that never wore a helmet. He was on the Ladenslager team.
I should have remembered that name, but I don't.
Yeah, well, he went into the electrical business then. But he wasn't in the small owls, huh?
Huh? He wasn't in the small owls.
No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. So, Errol had left then. And he took a band for a little while at the Embassy Club.
Also at the Suburban Gardens, didn't he?

Well, that was the Embassy Club. Oh, okay. Yeah, Embassy Club before it was the Suburban Gardens. And that was his, so I, then of course they all did, no, they all died except Rene and myself. And the last time I saw Rene was, he was getting out of the Canal bus. And as he was passing by, I said, hello, Rene. He says, oh, how are you doing? But the bus is stopped waiting for him to get out. That's the only thing he said was, hello.
Well, Benji White's still alive.
Oh, yeah, Benji. I used to see Benji occasionally.
And Dick Mackey.

Well, Dick, the last time I saw Dick has been a couple of years, but then I've seen Dick. And he's probably still as skinny as ever. And, but Dick went along to play with some out of town bands. Dick was well thought of as a trumpet player. And, but he didn't want to play professionally on here. That's the story that I got. I don't know that, and I know Red, well Red didn't want to play. Red wanted to be a big shot. He wanted to hang around the stock market and see what that is.
Were anybody in your family musicals, anybody? Besides you?
No, there's Rene Netto. His dad was a cousin of mine. That's the only one that I know. You've probably heard of Rene. Yeah. Well, Rene's daddy is a cousin of mine, but I never see Rene.
And the father didn't play anything? My father, no.
Yeah.
Sisters or brother?
He knew how to play race horses. Yeah. You know how to shoot dice.
Did you have any real idols when you were beginning to play? I mean, anybody that you admired, any trombonists? Like you listened to on a record or an impression, either one?
Well, T. Gordon, you know, everybody liked him. Everybody liked T. Gordon. Do you remember George Brunis? George Brunis?
Do you remember George Brunis? Oh yeah, I remember George, yeah. George. Well, George with Ted Lewis.

In fact I played with Ted Lewis down in the room there. But George wasn't there then. George had left him. He came down to New Orleans and he stayed by, and he went over to the Gulf Coast there, with a couple of bands. In fact I played a couple of jobs with him on the bass fiddle, you know, and he was playing some ball. George was not on, he didn't read music. He didn't know anything about music. In fact, who in the world was a worse pirate player than Ted Lewis. Sorry. He was fierce. And I was his official bass player. Whenever he came around in the air, Solly Klein used to run his band for him. Yeah, the violin player.
Huh?
Yeah, the violin player. And he used to send me a telegram. He was coming in the blue room on such and such a day. Be sure and be there.
Well, Ted Lewis hired good musicians, he should take that out of the house. He really did that.

Well, sometimes when he came in later on with the bands there, sometimes some of them weren't too good, you know. He didn't care much then. The only thing is, but he still loved to gamble, you know. He went over there. He held up the show for about 45 minutes one night. He was shooting dice in the one, two, three across the street from Roosevelt, and they sent for him over there, come on, the show's coming on. He said, wait a minute, I've got to make this eight. He went that eight and the shower door, and his wife used to travel with him. And she says, you have to pay the band. Because the band got their money, she had to take the band's money, and he says, no, the rest of it you can do what you want with it. But because Sally Klein threw him in, on Vegas, he says, over there, he says, he lost all of the salary, the band there, and what you call it, they had it sitting, freezing out there in the bus station waiting for New York to send them the money. Next morning, they couldn't get to New York at night time, so the office was closed, so they sent them the money the next morning.
Well you played with these bands when they came through. Did you travel with any of them? No, no, no.

So you stayed in town. In fact, I think I fell out with Al Hurt on the same deal when I played with Jumbo. Where did you play with Jumbo? Huh? Where did you play with him? I played with him when they opened up with Dan Levy's down there in that, what they called it, place on Bourbon Street there, that was one of my few stints on Bourbon Street. Toulouse and Bourbon? Yeah, he called it, not his club, the one before. Next door was a Chinese restaurant. Dan's International.
Dan's International, right. It was a Chinese restaurant, but I don't remember the name of the club.

The club was a ... I can find it, huh? They had nets on the bandstand and everything else and we had a black jacket. It wasn't something like Bayou. No, but it had something to that ... It was that kind of thing.
I know the Bayou Ball was in the wall of the Montietran or something.

I can't think of a ton of them. And whatchacar was playing for a bone in there and damn he was fine. And that guy would, well ... Oh, Bob Haven? Bob Haven, yeah. He played down there with him. Jumbo would take 30 choruses and Bob would take 40.
And the bass player would work in, work in, work in.

And then when he'd get finished, he'd say, take a cup. And he says, four beats, four beats, Frank, four beats. I said, for Christ's sake you're playing so fast I can't even play two. I said, whatchacar am I going to be playing? One.
You get to have a clarinet player?
Yeah, P. Fonten and ... Part of the hymn. And ... No, I'm ... Big tall fellow? Yeah, yeah. He plays a little out now.
Oh, you're thinking of ... Yeah, swing player. Tony DeFranco. Tony DeFranco. Tony Costa. Tony Costa.
Tony Costa. Yeah. Tony Costa.
Yeah. Tony Costa. Yeah.
I don't remember that. I really don't. Yeah, he was down there.

Yeah, he could have been, I just don't remember. Well, we only played down there Friday, Saturday, and Sunday. And they were playing a spot job crisis down there. And Dan, I was raised with Dan. I knew Dan from a kid up, Dan Levy. And I told him, I says, Dan, I says, we're not taking enough money to pay one person in the band. I said, how long are you going to take this beating? They'll come. Don't worry. They'll come. Dan was loaded, you know. And when he gets so, he'd get loaded and couldn't talk. He didn't talk. And he says, they'll be here. He says, you getting your money? Yeah. I said, yeah. I said, but after all, I said, you going to run out of money? He says, oh, so he kept on, kept on. Sure enough, they finally came. And, well, Jumbo, Jumbo, Jumbo, I told you, Jumbo, Pete, he put their brains in a head and he, well, before the mic, he'd fly backwards. We used to have that expression, the whistle through his ass. But he's a good guy. He's a good guy.
How long did you play with Jumbo?
Until he wanted to leave town and then he wanted me to leave to Roosevelt and go. I said, no, no. I said, hell no.
So you were playing during the day at the Roosevelt?

I was playing during the day. I was playing with Jordan Crest then. And then some, I said, I said, look, I said, I got a camp. I said, I can go sleep at the camp. I got a house. I said, I can go sleep at the house. And I'm going to go buy a bed in some other town. I said, and then get in, wait for the Standard Oil Company. I said, after all, they're buying gasoline, running around from here to there. So, yeah.
When was that? Was that in the 40s?
No, I think that was probably around the 60s. 60s, that late.
So you would play with Jumbo through the 50s then, huh?

Well, when Jumbo left, WWL if you remember that, I was playing with him then. No, I don't remember it. Because he signed up with, with, with, uh, Vicar, well, D'Antoni, when he opened up that place on, when he opened up that boxing club there that's on St. Charles and Poitras.
You know which club he's talking about, Dick? Curly's?

Curly's. Curly's Corner. He, uh, whatever. He, uh, he went in there and the first night we were in there, but you know how loud Jumbo blew. He told Jumbo, he says, for Christ's sake you're playing so loud I can't even think. So, uh, Jumbo says, Sarah, he says, I got a contract with this guy. He says, you gotta pay me. He says, he can't find me. He says, after all I quit WWL and everything else. So, here comes two ladies down in the bar over there and some guy's wife, I don't know who it was, D'Antoni went over there. He says, look, he said, I'm gonna tell you right down, there ain't no hoes gonna be around over here. And, uh, they had quite a big of them. Godfrey Hirsch. Yeah, I believe it was Godfrey. I said, Godfrey, I said, we better get the hell out of here. I said, they're gonna wind up there and somebody's gonna shoot somebody and I said, they're gonna miss them and hit us. How long had you known Godfrey at that point? I knew Godfrey from back when I was, he used to play a night when he was going to school. He played drums with Godfrey. He used to play a night when he was going to school. He played drums. He was playing drums with us, yeah. When Crum would take off a night now and then, Godfrey would play for us.
Godfrey was younger than you.
Oh, yeah. Godfrey was about 76, 77. About five years. He was 15, 16 years old. He was going to school. He went to Tulane, but how long? I don't know.
He graduated.
He graduated?
He played in the Tulaneans.
Well, he played in the Tulaneans until he was 80 years, until he was 70 years old.
Oh, who took your place with Hurt? Bob Coquille. Well, Bob, I interviewed Bob a couple of times. He had a wonderful memory for Tate, so we could check.
Well, my God, he could beat me. Well, Bob's dead now, isn't he?
Yeah. Yeah, but we have it on tape.
Yeah. So, at least I hope. He took my place there. He cut a couple of records with him, too. I believe Jumbo's still losing for him.
Did you do any recording with Jumbo?
No, I didn't make any records with Jumbo. I recorded with Amarillo.
You did? Yeah.

How long did you play with Tony? Oh, I played with Tony... During the war, I was with him. I played on a Capitol Ave with him. You made the records then? We made a few records, but I never heard of them coming out anywhere.
That'd be worth looking up.

See if they... Oh, I wouldn't look them up because this guy, Mares... Well, you know, he and Pete... Pete and Al hate each other. There's no question about it, but they get together every now and then and make a buck. But then... And Mares stole the records from them and turned them out. And I don't know the whole story of it. But he's been known for Duda, that Mares guy. Now his brother, the trumpet... Paul. Yeah, Paul. I don't know too much of him either.
I wanted to ask you about these kids that you taught in the Western Union Band. Did any of them grow up to be professionals?

There was a boy, Martyr. He played piano in a couple of places. And to my knowledge, I don't think any of the others did. But then... Maurice took the item band. In fact, the item wanted me to take the band. I said, no. I said, one of them is driving me crazy. I said, I ain't going to get another one. So Maurice took it. And he happened to get Eddie Miller. So Eddie Miller was the product out of those two bands.
Well how did you pronounce Eddie Miller's name then?
Eddie Miller?
He was Miller then?
Yes, Miller now isn't it?

Yeah, now, but it used to be Mula, Mala. I didn't know that. Some German guy told me that. He met him and it turned out his name was a German name. I think when he was in America it became Miller. Yeah, well he was hit from here.

Because I remember when he used to come to play his saxophone on a bandstand and he'd have a hole in his pants I'd say for a minute. Ormond hug. When Ormond, we got a hole in Ormond, Eddie said get Ormond, he said as a piano player, when Chris left, Sid Christensen. He says get Ormond hug. He says he's alright. He says okay, okay. So we went to a hole and Ormond came there with his uncle, Will Badinko. You know that name?
I know the name.

I know the name. Yeah, he used to be an entertainer of some sort down there in the quarter. So he came down there with, sitting in a band, a rehearsal, and he'd come in there with a mustache and short pants. And I told him, I said, he sat down there and played and I said, well Ormond, I said one of them's got to go. Either short pants or got to go. So Bill and I were running the band at the time, Bill Padron. And we were splitting the liter price and that's how the argument wound up later. I said it don't make a difference. After all he told me, he says, well he says he can't afford to pay the whole price over the time. And I said, I said, well what are you going to do? I said, he says, well let's give in to him for a couple of weeks. We'll look for another job. So about two weeks after that he gets sick on a pay night. So Pete gave me the money. He gave me the full price. And I went up to the hospital and I said, I said, Bill, I said, Pete gave me all the money. He says, oh, he says, I told you that because my wife's daughter was going to, which wasn't his, he said that daughter was going to graduate and they needed a few extra bucks. I said, you said, what? I said, you ought to have told me that. I said, I would have gave you the money. I said, but you, he's in the hospital. I said, but now you're best and I hope you die. And that's when he got out there, I quit the band. I told him, I said, no, I said, I had enough of that.
I'm curious to ask, do you happen to remember a cornet player named Emmet Hardy?
Yeah, Emmet Hardy. Fine.
Fine player. He never recorded.
I think he was a, I think he was, no, no, no, I mean between white and black. I don't know whether, no, no, he wasn't queer.
As I understand, he dated one of the Boswell sisters. He dated her? He dated, I think Martha.

I mean, it could have been, but then Zito knows him better than I do. And Zito is the one that told me, he says, man, he says, Emmet, it's a little dark, you know. Yeah, well, what the hell, he might love being a little dark. He said, he ain't got, now Zito, he's like, that might have come out of the sky, you know. But Emmet was from across the road, in that section over there where they had those little coffee and a cake, coffee and a milk, you know. In Algiers? Yeah, yeah. Can you remember hearing him play? Yeah, he played fine. He played fine, no question about it.
Would it be possible to ask, some have said that Emmet Hardy had a great deal of influence on Bix Beiderbecke? Do you remember Beiderbecke's playing in the game?
I've heard that, I've heard that. I've heard that, that Beiderbecke listened to Hardy quite a bit.
I don't know whether he'd be able to remember if there was any similarity in their playing. I consider it unlikely myself.
Well, I'll tell you, I don't think. I really don't think. But everybody that knew around here thought that Hardy had more possibilities than anybody.
Speaking of influences.

In fact, Louis Armstrong used to listen to Hardy. Is that so? Yeah. I knew Louis, Louis was kind of a nigger if he ever was one. His aunt lived about four doors from me on, on Clavin Avenue. It was a mixed neighborhood down there. Mrs. Stella Armstrong, she was a midwife. It was back in the days when they had those gals that brought in the babies. And I said, well, Joe Maselli was, I went to school with Joe. And Joe used to idolize. He tried to play Louis and everything else. But Louis was in the waif's home and in jail more often than he was out. And she's come over there one time over there. I says, how's Louis? I had Louis become famous then. And she says, you know, she says, that little nigger, she says, he's calling those tunes, his tunes. And I sang them to him when he was a baby. His aunt said that. And my stepmother told me, she says, yeah, she says, she's criticizing Louis. And Louis is giving her $15 a month. And that's her rent money. He's paying her rent money.
Well, Louis went on to play with a band that seems to have had some influence on you guys and the ailes. Fletcher Henderson? Yeah, yeah. Did you listen a lot to Fletcher Henderson?

Yeah, we listened to Fletcher Henderson and that other band from Canada up there. What was the name of that? You know? Canada? I think they were, well, I don't know if they were Canadians, but they were playing up in Canada. Radio came in around 20- Is this a black group? No, I don't believe. I don't believe. Oh, Christ. Godfrey had some of these recordings over there. I thought they were terrific.
Was this before the Casa Luma was organized? Yeah, before Casa Luma. Before Gene Goldcat? That's the one. Gene Goldcat.
Gene Goldcat. Gene Goldcat. I thought that they were terrific.
Did they have a good bass player? Huh? Did they have a good bass player?
Well, I wasn't paying much attention to bass, but I was listening to the old band.
The bass player was from New Orleans, Steve Brown. Do you remember him? I heard of him.

I didn't know him. I heard of him. He left here before. He played with the rhythm keys. Yeah. But back in those days, they wanted to be steady and swing, you know, just a little emphasis on that third beat, on the second and fourth beat, rather. Yeah. And... Syncopation?
Huh?
Yeah. Syncopation today, huh? Yeah.

Yeah. You had a couple of interesting things that happened recording-wise with Fletcher Henderson songs. You did Dynamite on the same day. You recorded Dynamite in this town on the same day that Henderson recorded it in New York. Did you know that?
No, I didn't know that. But then that's why they took Henderson's record. Yours was released, too.

Huh? Yours was also released. Yours was released, too. Yeah. Do you have any idea how that came to be? Not the slightest idea. Was it pure coincidence, or...? Absolutely, pure coincidence. Was there any connection with a manager that...?

Not that I know of. No, no. No, Earl Crumb would have to answer that. Uh-huh. Because Earl Crumb handled all the... We told him, we'll go ahead, whatever you do is okay. And that was one orchestra that we never took a drink on the bassinet. Was that right? And, uh, we... In fact, I went through my whole career that way. Because I said, if they're paying for us... If they're paying us to play, I said, we'll have a good time. If you want a drink... I never drank. I drank more after I retired. One drink twice a week, probably. And, uh, I... Before that, I never took a drink of that in no time. A guy walked through, I said, I got some trouble. I can't take it. So that's ended it. But I never took a drink on the bassinet. And that, Earl's Orchestra, none of them did either.
Do you remember how you got to know about a song like Dynamite, since Henderson hadn't recorded it yet for you to hear it?
No. I think the only... The only possibility would have been Chris, the piano player, would have got down there with... But he and Pinky would be the only two guys that would...
Would they have been to New York and heard Henderson play it?
No, they were down here with us. Yeah.
That's what I'm curious is to know how... How... No. You guys even knew about the song. Did you have an arrangement? Huh?
Did you have arrangements?
Most of our tunes, no. We played together and memorized them as we went along. And we'd stop now and then, you know, and tell the guy, well, wait a minute, we can do this and do that and do that.
Were there some stock arrangements that you guys had?

Well, we used to play some stock over on the band, you know, on what you call them, but then we got the last tunes of the set. If they were dancing, that's a... You know, you played the same old... But like it's just...
You had a stock arrangement on it already?
I don't ever recall having a stock arrangement on it. We could have been, but then I'm not... I'm not...
I'm not positive. Pretty standard stock arrangements. Arrangements pretty much like the stock of the time. Tampico and Dynamite both are very much... . . . .
We got the third reel on now, Rene Netto.
I missed all that now. Did Rene Jalpe ever play guitar?
To my knowledge, no. I don't think Rene would play guitar. Not with us, anyway, if he went along there. But you said that they had two.
